title: Roger Stone email claimed he dined with Julian Assange; a meeting was disputed
description_medium: On August 4, 2016, Roger Stone emailed that he had dined with WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange the previous night. Stone later denied meeting him and said travel records placed him in Los Angeles and Miami, not London. The email establishes Stone’s claim, not a physical meeting or proof that he coordinated with Russia.
description_long: On August 4, 2016, Roger Stone sent an email saying he had dined with WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange the previous night. CNN reported that Stone made the claim on the same day he predicted damaging WikiLeaks disclosures about Hillary Clinton’s foundation. The email prompted questions because Assange was in London and Stone later said airline and credit-card records placed him in Los Angeles and Miami; Stone denied having met Assange. The available evidence therefore establishes that Stone made the claim, but it does not confirm a physical dinner. The original headline treats the dinner as an event and adds that Stone began “covering for Russia.” That phrase asserts both a meeting and a motive not demonstrated by the cited account. Stone’s public comments about expected WikiLeaks material are relevant context, but they do not by themselves establish that he received information from Assange or acted in coordination with Russian officials.

corrected_wording.title: Roger Stone email claimed he dined with Julian Assange; a meeting was disputed

source_access_notes: CNN’s reporting on Stone’s August 2016 email and his subsequent denial was retrieved. The supplied TrumpFile page’s physical-meeting claim is not independently confirmed by that account.
blockers: No independent evidence in the supplied record confirms that Stone and Assange met in person or establishes that Stone’s statements were made to cover for Russia.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: James Comey testified that voting systems were not connected to the internet
description_medium: On September 28, 2016, FBI Director James Comey told Congress that actual voting systems were decentralized and not connected to the internet. He separately acknowledged scanning and attempted access to voter-registration systems in several states. The testimony supports that distinction; the supplied material does not show that Comey knowingly lied.
description_long: FBI Director James Comey testified before the House Judiciary Committee on September 28, 2016, about cyber activity targeting election systems. He described scanning and attempted intrusions aimed at voter-registration sites in more than a dozen states, while saying that actual voting systems were decentralized and not connected to the internet. The distinction matters: voter-registration databases and vote-counting equipment are different parts of election infrastructure. The Election Assistance Commission’s summary of findings likewise distinguished registration databases from vote-counting systems. Contemporary reporting said investigators had not found that information was changed or that voting systems were at risk. The supplied title calls Comey a liar, but the materials provided do not establish that his statement about voting machines was knowingly false. They support an account of his testimony and the separate targeting of registration systems, not a conclusion about his intent. Comey said the bureau found no indication that vote tallies had changed.

corrected_wording.title: James Comey testified that voting systems were not connected to the internet

source_access_notes: CNN’s hearing coverage and an Election Assistance Commission briefing on 2016 election cybersecurity were retrieved. They distinguish voter-registration systems from vote-counting equipment.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: NRA ad spending drew allegations of coordination with Trump’s 2016 campaign
description_medium: Reporting on the NRA’s 2016 spending described overlapping television ad purchases by NRA and Trump campaign media firms, including shared vendors and timing. Former FEC chair Ann Ravel called the arrangement apparent illegal coordination. A commissioner’s statement in the FEC matter says a proposed “reason to believe” finding was not adopted; the record does not establish a final legal finding of coordination.
description_long: The National Rifle Association spent heavily to support Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign, and investigative reporting later examined how its television advertising was arranged. The Trace and Mother Jones reported that the NRA and Trump campaign purchased pro-Trump placements for the same dates and networks through firms connected to National Media. Former Federal Election Commission chair Ann Ravel, after reviewing records, called the arrangement apparent illegal coordination. That is an expert assessment of the evidence, not itself an agency ruling. In a related FEC matter, a commissioner’s statement says the commission’s general counsel recommended a “reason to believe” finding based on alleged coordinated communications, but the commission did not adopt that proposed analysis. A preliminary threshold finding would not itself establish a violation. The record supports reporting the overlapping purchases and the ensuing allegations, while the title’s assertion that illegal coordination was conclusively established goes beyond the material.

corrected_wording.title: NRA ad spending drew allegations of coordination with Trump’s 2016 campaign

source_access_notes: The Trace investigation and FEC statement in MUR 7427 were retrieved. The FEC document explains that proposed findings were not adopted and that a “reason to believe” threshold does not itself establish a violation.
blockers: The supplied sources do not establish a final FEC or court finding that the NRA and Trump campaign illegally coordinated their advertising.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: Debt-ceiling warnings described a hypothetical crisis, not a U.S. default
description_medium: A 2023 Peterson Foundation article warned that rising debt-service costs and a congressional debt-ceiling standoff could threaten federal payments. A separate 2025 analysis modeled how Project 2025’s proposed limits on financial regulators might worsen a future crisis. These sources describe fiscal risks and a hypothetical scenario; they do not report a U.S. default, recession, or the specific losses asserted in the headline.
description_long: The sources behind this entry describe fiscal risks, not a national default. In 2023, the Peter G. Peterson Foundation reported that federal debt had reached $33.6 trillion and interest costs had risen to $879 billion in fiscal year 2023. It warned that a debt-ceiling standoff could bring the country to the brink of missed payments and credit-rating damage. A separate Center for American Progress analysis argued that Project 2025 proposals limiting the Federal Reserve’s emergency lending role could make a future financial crisis harder to contain. Neither account says the United States defaulted on its debt in 2025. Nor do they report the claimed three million job losses, higher mortgage costs, recession, or $850 billion increase in debt as consequences of an actual default. The event as preserved in the title is not supported; the substantiated material concerns debt-service pressures and a modeled risk if Congress or regulators fail to respond to a future crisis.

corrected_wording.title: Debt-ceiling warnings described a hypothetical crisis, not a U.S. default

source_access_notes: The Peterson Foundation debt-risk article and Center for American Progress analysis were retrieved. They describe a 2023 debt-ceiling warning and a hypothetical financial-crisis scenario under proposed policy changes.
blockers: The cited sources do not document a 2025 default or the headline’s claimed economic losses; a specific realized default event is unsupported.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: Rybolovlev’s plane shared airports with Trump’s campaign jet twice
description_medium: During the 2016 campaign, Dmitry Rybolovlev’s plane and Donald Trump’s campaign aircraft were reported at the same airports in Las Vegas and Charlotte on separate days. Rybolovlev’s adviser called the overlap coincidental, and both men denied meeting. The flight records show shared airport locations, not an encounter or communication between them.
description_long: In the final week of the 2016 presidential campaign, flight-tracking records showed Dmitry Rybolovlev’s aircraft and Donald Trump’s campaign jet at the same airports on separate occasions. Reports identified an overlap in Las Vegas on October 30 and another around Trump’s Charlotte rally on November 3. The timing drew attention because Rybolovlev is a Russian billionaire and Trump’s campaign was under scrutiny for its Russia connections. Rybolovlev’s adviser said the intersecting travel was coincidental and that Rybolovlev had never met Trump; Trump also denied meeting him. The evidence concerns the aircraft’s presence at airports, not a confirmed meeting between the two men. A title saying the men “cross paths” can suggest a personal encounter, so the more precise account identifies the planes and the limited nature of the records. No communication or coordination is established by the reported flight overlap.

corrected_wording.title: Rybolovlev’s plane shared airports with Trump’s campaign jet twice

source_access_notes: Charlotte Observer reporting was retrieved and confirms reported airport overlaps and the adviser’s denial that Rybolovlev had met Trump.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: Trump order removed bargaining coverage for selected federal agencies
description_medium: On March 27, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14251, excluding 40 federal agencies and subdivisions from labor-management relations statutes. The order narrowed collective-bargaining coverage for employees in the listed organizations; it did not eliminate unions across public and private employment or ban private-sector organizing.
description_long: Executive Order 14251, issued on March 27, 2025, excluded 40 federal agencies and subdivisions from the federal labor-management relations statutes. Those statutes provide collective-bargaining rights for most federal employees. The order cited national-security responsibilities and directed that employees in the listed agencies no longer receive coverage under the relevant bargaining framework. Congressional Research Service analysis describes the order as affecting selected federal agencies, not the entire federal workforce. The order therefore changed labor protections for employees in specified parts of the government; it did not abolish federal unions across all agencies, end collective bargaining in state and local government, or make private-sector organizing illegal. Separate policy proposals in Project 2025 could further alter labor rules, but those proposals should not be conflated with the scope of this executive order. The documented action was a targeted exclusion from federal labor-management relations programs, with the legal reach tied to the agencies and subdivisions named by the administration.

corrected_wording.title: Trump order removed bargaining coverage for selected federal agencies

source_access_notes: The White House executive order and Congressional Research Service analysis were retrieved; CRS identifies 40 agencies and subdivisions excluded from the federal labor-management statutes.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: New York withheld Vitaly Churkin’s autopsy findings after a State Department request
description_medium: After Russian ambassador Vitaly Churkin died in New York in February 2017, the city medical examiner said it could not disclose the cause and manner of death. NBC News reported that the State Department barred release under an international-law rationale. The available coverage documents the withholding; it does not show that Trump directed it.
description_long: Vitaly Churkin, Russia’s ambassador to the United Nations, died in New York on February 20, 2017. The New York City medical examiner said it could not disclose the cause and manner of his death, and NBC News reported that the State Department barred release of the autopsy information. Contemporary reporting described the federal government’s position as based on international law and Russia’s objections to disclosure. This establishes a decision to withhold the findings and the stated legal rationale reported at the time. The supplied timeline headline places the episode in a Trump-Russia frame, but the cited account does not establish that President Trump directed the request or influenced the medical examiner’s decision. The event can be described as a federal request or restriction affecting a city medical examiner’s release of information about a foreign diplomat’s death; claims about the President’s role or political motive require separate evidence.

corrected_wording.title: New York withheld Vitaly Churkin’s autopsy findings after a State Department request

source_access_notes: NBC News reporting was retrieved and states that the State Department barred release; the BBC search result reports the medical examiner’s international-law explanation. The supplied page does not establish Trump’s role.
blockers: No evidence in the supplied sources shows that Trump directed or influenced the State Department’s request.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: Trump order revised military readiness rules; it did not mandate youth training
description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Trump issued an executive order directing the Defense Department to revise military service standards and policies related to gender dysphoria. The order addressed military personnel and readiness. The supplied sources do not describe mandatory school ASVAB testing, youth service, military camps, or ideological training for students.
description_long: President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14183, “Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness,” on January 27, 2025. The order directed the Defense Department to revise standards for military service and to rescind policies it considered inconsistent with readiness, including guidance related to gender dysphoria and pronoun use. A White House fact sheet described the order as changing eligibility and service policies for transgender-identifying people in the military. The supplied Task & Purpose article discusses separate Project 2025 recommendations for the Pentagon. Neither source establishes a national youth-service program, mandatory military training camps, or a requirement that every high school student take the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery. Those claims in the original description are unsupported. The order focused on military eligibility standards and personnel policy. The event documented here concerns military personnel policy and readiness, not a youth training or school curriculum mandate.

corrected_wording.title: Trump order revised military readiness rules; it did not mandate youth training

source_access_notes: The supplied White House order and Task & Purpose link were checked; the direct page retrieval was blank for both, but White House search results identify the order’s focus on military standards and service policy.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: Project 2025 favors heterosexual-family policies but does not propose ending marriage equality
description_medium: A 2024 fact-check found that Project 2025 does not propose ending same-sex marriage. The plan describes heterosexual families as ideal and seeks protections for faith-based federal grant recipients that oppose same-sex marriage. The supplied sources do not describe a federal annulment program or a repeal of marriage recognition.
description_long: The claim that Project 2025 would create a federal program to annul same-sex marriages is not supported by the cited sources. A 2024 PolitiFact review found that the policy document does not propose ending same-sex marriage. It does describe heterosexual, two-parent families as an ideal and calls for protections for faith-based organizations receiving federal grants, including organizations that oppose same-sex marriage. Other Project 2025 proposals could reduce protections for LGBTQ+ people in areas such as health care, education, and federal civil-rights policy, but those changes are distinct from a federal program to void existing marriages. The materials supplied for this entry identify no executive action to withdraw federal recognition of marriage equality and no mechanism for states to annul marriages already performed. A precise account should distinguish the plan’s conservative family-policy and religious-liberty recommendations from the unsupported claim that it proposed ending marriage equality.

corrected_wording.title: Project 2025 favors heterosexual-family policies but does not propose ending marriage equality

source_access_notes: PolitiFact and GLAAD materials were located; PolitiFact’s search-result summary directly states that Project 2025 does not propose ending same-sex marriage and describes its heterosexual-family and faith-based-grant positions.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.

title: Trump administration did not impose new CAATSA sanctions on Russia by January 2018
description_medium: On January 29, 2018, the Trump administration did not impose new sanctions under Section 231 of CAATSA against Russian entities. State Department officials said that date began the law’s sanctions authority rather than setting a deadline and argued that the threat had already deterred transactions. The decision did not mean that every Russia-related sanction under the law was ignored.
description_long: The Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), enacted in 2017, authorized sanctions against people and entities involved in significant transactions with Russia’s defense and intelligence sectors. On January 29, 2018, the Trump administration did not announce new sanctions under Section 231. State Department officials said the date was the beginning of the period in which the law authorized sanctions, not a deadline requiring the administration to impose them that day. They also argued that publication of a list of Russian officials and entities and the threat of sanctions had deterred some transactions. Members of Congress criticized the decision, saying the administration had failed to carry out the law’s intended pressure on Russia. The documented episode is a dispute over whether the administration should have designated specific people or companies under Section 231. It does not show that the administration refused to enforce every part of CAATSA or that Congress had already imposed a specific set of sanctions that the president then canceled.

corrected_wording.title: Trump administration did not impose new CAATSA sanctions on Russia by January 2018

source_access_notes: State Department’s Section 231 briefing and Congressional Research Service sanctions report were identified; the State Department search result says January 29 was not a deadline to impose sanctions but the start date for Section 231 authorities.
rationale: Describes the substantiated action or claim, distinguishes allegations from findings, and corrects unsupported causal or legal conclusions.
